targets.outcome_quote: Our results provide mixed evidence regarding the role of extremal edges defined by texture alone in depth perception. In our data, EE2 (a region with an extremal edge on the shared contour, and on the opposite contour) was chosen as closer than other textures, paralleling the original study. Likewise, when both regions had only one extremal edge, the one with the extremal edge on the shared contour was more likely to be perceived as closer (EE1>Convex1), though this effect was weaker than in the original study. However, we were unsuccessful in replicating the finding that EE1 regions are perceived as closer then Convex2 surfaces; this test asks whether an extremal edge on the shared contour is the dominant cue to depth in these stimuli, when pitted against the number of extremal edges (i.e. half cylinders are seen as close than quarter cylinders), and so constitutes a stringent test of the prediction.

targets.evidence_quote: Replication of “What Do Cross-National Comparisons of Personality Traits Tell Us? The Case of Conscientiousness” by SJ Heine, EE Buchtel, A Norenzayan (2008, Psychological Science).
targets.outcome_quote: We successfully replicated the original findings of Heine, et al. (2008). Results from our replication show that validity criteria (behavioural and demographic measures of conscientiousness) have significant correlations with Perceptions of National Characters (PNC), but not with self- and peer-report measures of conscientiousness. In other words, this replication study adds confirming evidence to the claim of Heine et al. (2008) that unlike personality measures, PNC is related to societal behavioural indicators of conscientiousness. Inclusion of additional global societal indicator of conscientiousness, i.e., Fragile State Index, showed very similar relations with personality and PNC measures as other indices used in study.

targets.title: Detecting the snake in the grass: attention to fear-relevant stimuli by adults and young children
targets.evidence_quote: Replication of Detecting the Snake in the Grass: Attention to Fear-Relevant Stimuli by Adults and Young Children by Vanessa LoBue and Judy S. DeLoache (2008, Psychological Science) Replicating Authors: Leslie D. Cramblet Alvarez & R. Nathan Pipitone Professor & Assistant Professor of Psychology Student Research Assistants: Tylar Martinez, Megan Tapia & Kellylynn Zuni Adams State University Alamosa, Colorado
targets.outcome_quote: The current study attempted to replicate LoBue and DeLoache’s (2008) Experiment 3 finding that children and adults found fear-relevant stimuli (a snake among caterpillars) more quickly than visually similar fear-irrelevant stimuli (a caterpillar among snakes). While both children and adults’ reaction times were faster for fear-relevant conditions, and, we were able to approximate the original study’s sample size, we were unable to attain statistical significance in our replication for the original publication’s Experiment 3 key finding. Lobue and Deloache (2008) reported a significant main effect for target stimulus with a sizeable effect size (η2 = .23), meaning 23% of the variance in reaction time could be explained as a function of which condition participants were in. Our effect size for the main effect of condition was η2 = .032, or only 3.2% of the variance in reaction time could be explained as a function of participant condition.

targets.outcome_quote: We found a negative, nonsignificant effect of endowment category on underestimation of the frequency of pictures belonging to that category. This finding directly contradicts those of the original study by Dai and colleagues, which stated that pictures belonging to the endowment category should be judged to be relatively less frequent than those belonging to the other category.
